elements.element: Customer is not required to pay any liquidated damages.
elements.evidence: The redlined clause deletes the USD 25,000-per-day liquidated-damages obligation and provides only timeline relief and recovery of reasonable, documented, unavoidable costs directly caused by actual delay.

elements.element: Customer is not required to pay any penalties.
elements.evidence: The redlined clause imposes no penalty on Customer; the permitted cost recovery is compensatory and tied to documented costs directly caused by the delay.

elements.element: Any liquidated amount payable by Customer is limited to an early-termination fee.
elements.evidence: No liquidated amount is payable by Customer under the redlined clause, so the condition for this limitation is demonstrably absent.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee payable by Customer is capped at three months' fees.
elements.evidence: The redlined clause contains no early-termination fee, so the condition for applying the cap is demonstrably absent.

elements.element: An early-termination fee is the sole liquidated amount that may be payable by Customer.
elements.evidence: The redlined clause permits no liquidated amount of any kind, which is more protective than permitting a sole early-termination liquidated amount.

result.reason: The operative language fully removes liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer, satisfying the preferred position and therefore also the fallback limitations. It is not minimal because, beyond deleting the liquidated-damages obligation, it adds affirmative schedule-extension and cost-recovery rights. Those additions are related to the same delay risk and do not disturb unrelated commercial terms, but “equitable extension” is somewhat vague and the clause does not specify a procedure for documenting or claiming costs.
